ai-at-work.title: AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says
ai-at-work.excerpt: "Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech."
ai-at-work.dwp_take: A top economist at Apollo Global Management looked at the numbers and found that most companies investing heavily in AI haven't seen any actual financial returns yet. This matters because digital workplace leaders are getting pressure from executives to deploy AI everywhere, and this research suggests those investments might not deliver the ROI that justifies the spend. After thirty years watching technology trends come and go, I'd say this is a healthy dose of reality for a field that's been riding pure hype instead of results, and it's worth showing this data to anyone trying to sell you an AI solution that promises miracles.

ai-at-work.title: Apollo analysis shows no one besides the biggest tech giants is seeing benefits from AI
ai-at-work.excerpt: Despite all of the hype and the multiple millions of dollars invested in artificial intelligence, most of corporate America outside of its biggest technology firms is yet to see any financial payoff,
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Apollo Global Management's analysis found that despite massive AI investments, only the biggest tech giants are actually seeing financial returns while most other companies aren't benefiting yet. This matters to digital workplace pros because it means the AI tools you're being pressured to roll out might not deliver the ROI your leadership is expecting, which could affect budgets and priorities down the road. Here's the thing: if you're in a mid-market company getting pitched yet another AI solution, you're basically being sold a lottery ticket while the house keeps the winnings.

ai-at-work.title: Elon Musk predicts neocloud shakeout as credit for AI infrastructure dries up
ai-at-work.excerpt: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. Chief Executive Elon Musk revealed his company has secured $40 billion in debt financing in order to purchase powerful chips for artificial intelligence workloads.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Musk just signaled that neocloud startups are about to hit a funding wall, with his company securing $40 billion in debt to buy AI chips while others will struggle to raise capital. This matters because it tells us the infrastructure layer of AI is consolidating fast, meaning your company's AI vendor options are shrinking and pricing power is shifting to the big players. The real story here is that we're watching the venture-backed cool kids get crushed by reality, and only the players with access to massive debt markets will survive, which is basically the opposite of how tech was supposed to work.

ai-at-work.excerpt: Will bringing automation into the financial industry prove disastrous or transformative? Intuit Inc., the financial technology company behind Credit Karma, QuickBooks and TurboTax, sees artificial int
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Intuit is hosting Connect on October 28 to showcase how AI is reshaping financial software, moving workflows from manual data entry toward automated planning and analysis. Digital workplace pros need to watch this because financial teams are early adopters of AI automation, and whatever Intuit demos will likely influence enterprise adoption timelines across other departments. Here's the thing though: moving from manual reconciliation to "proactive financial planning" sounds great until someone realizes AI hallucinated next quarter's budget.

digital-culture.title: Why quitting your job might be your best decision yet
digital-culture.excerpt: Below, Lindsay Crouse shares five key insights from her new book, The Case for Quitting: The Surprising Benefits of Opting Out. Lindsay is a marathon runner and journalist who worked at The New York T
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece featuring journalist Lindsay Crouse's new book arguing that quitting isn't failure but rather a strategic decision to abandon goals that no longer serve you. For digital workplace folks, this matters because we spend so much time optimizing retention and engagement that we rarely ask whether people should actually stay. Here's the thing though: most organizations won't care about this book until they figure out why good people are leaving in the first place, and spoiler alert, it's usually not because they didn't read enough self-help.

digital-culture.title: Hiring program in energy tech sector enlists military veterans to fill data center skills gap
digital-culture.excerpt: With an unprecedented surge in demand for skilled technicians, Schneider Electric eyes talent with military experience.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Schneider Electric is specifically recruiting military veterans to fill open data center technician roles as demand for skilled workers outpaces supply in the energy tech sector. This matters because it signals how serious skills shortages have become - companies are now looking beyond traditional talent pipelines and recognizing that military training translates directly to technical competency. Here's the thing though: this should have happened years ago, and it took a crisis to make it obvious that veterans are a goldmine of discipline, problem-solving ability, and hands-on technical experience that most hiring managers were simply overlooking.

industry-news.title: This Week in Tech: AI Agents Clock In as Apple Buyers Wait and IT Scrambles
industry-news.excerpt: See what you missed in Daily Tech Insider from Oct. 19–23. The post This Week in Tech: AI Agents Clock In as Apple Buyers Wait and IT Scrambles appeared first on TechRepublic.
industry-news.dwp_take: AI agents are moving into workplace automation while Apple customers sit tight waiting for new products, leaving IT teams caught between adopting emerging tools and managing existing infrastructure. This matters because digital workplace leaders need to figure out right now whether AI agents are a genuine productivity play or just the latest shiny object that'll require a budget ask and three months of troubleshooting. My bet is most organizations will do both: some teams will go all-in on agents while IT scrambles to govern what they're actually doing, which sounds familiar because we've done this dance before with every new technology since email.

industry-news.title: A spate of cyber attacks has rocked Japan
industry-news.excerpt: With over 100 cyber attacks impacting major sectors this year, Japan’s ruling party is calling for an emergency taskforce to strengthen AI defenses
industry-news.dwp_take: Japan's facing a wave of cyber attacks across major sectors this year, prompting the ruling party to push for an emergency taskforce focused on AI-powered defenses. For digital workplace pros, this is a reminder that security infrastructure can't be an afterthought when you're scaling remote work and cloud adoption. Here's the thing though: no amount of AI wizardry stops an employee from clicking a suspicious link, so Japan might want to pair that taskforce with some old-fashioned security training while they're at it.
